title: The Last of the Old Guard: San Francisco's New Delhi Restaurant Wins a Place in History
excerpt: A 38-year-old Indian institution becomes one of just 50 U.S. eateries to land a Backing Historic Small Restaurants grant — and the only Indian-owned business on the city's legacy registry.
body:
In a restaurant industry where the opening of a buzzy new spot is often the only constant, survival is its own kind of triumph. New Delhi Restaurant, which has anchored San Francisco's dining scene since 1988, has just been recognized for exactly that — named one of only 50 eateries across the United States to win this year's Backing Historic Small Restaurants grant from the National Trust for Historic Preservation and American Express.

## A patriarch, not a trend

New Delhi was a sensation the moment it opened. Within a couple of years it had become a magnet for Indian celebrities and American luminaries alike — Deepak Chopra, Anthony Hopkins, Julia Child — and President Bill Clinton stopped by during both of his campaigns. Its Maharaja-style banquet dining room offered a vision of Indian hospitality that the city had rarely seen.

Founder Ranjan Dey was, in many ways, a prototype for today's celebrity chefs. By 1990, with his restaurant ranked among the best Indian establishments in the country by The New York Times, he had launched his own line of New World Spices — each tin celebrating the story of a famous Indian figure. Warm, buoyant and deeply knowledgeable, Dey radiated the kind of personal brand that the industry would later commodify.

## Context and background

New Delhi's recognition carries an extra weight: of the 461 listings on the San Francisco Registry of Legacy Businesses, it is the only one owned and operated by an Indian entrepreneur. That statistic says as much about the precariousness of immigrant-run restaurants as it does about Dey's staying power. Many of the mom-and-pop Indian spots that opened in the same era have closed, squeezed by rent, succession struggles and a competitive climate that rewards reinvention over endurance.

The grant lands at a moment of paradox for Indian food in America. At the high end, Michelin-starred chefs and U.K. imports like Dishoom are redefining the cuisine for a new, affluent audience. But the institutions that did the early, unglamorous work — introducing Americans to a full Indian menu decades before it was fashionable — are quietly disappearing. New Delhi's award is a recognition that this groundwork matters.

## Diaspora impact

For the Bay Area's Indian community, New Delhi is more than a restaurant; it is a landmark of belonging. It opened when the diaspora was far smaller and far less visible, and it became a place where immigrants could host American friends and bosses with pride rather than apology. To have it formally preserved — its facade mural by artist Kenneth Cook set to be restored with grant funds — is to have a piece of diaspora history written into the city's permanent record.

The recognition also reframes what "legacy" means for immigrant businesses. The grant is not for the trendiest room or the most influencer-friendly plate, but for the dependable patriarch families keep returning to across generations. For NRIs who grew up watching their parents' restaurants struggle to be taken seriously, the honor is a form of overdue respect — proof that staying, serving and feeding a community for nearly four decades is itself a contribution worth memorializing.

## What's next

The Backing Historic Small Restaurants grant will help fund the mural's restoration and other improvements, but its larger value is symbolic: it places New Delhi back in the local and national spotlight just as a new generation rediscovers it. As flashier Indian concepts chase Michelin stars and venture capital, New Delhi's award is a reminder that the cuisine's American story did not begin with the current boom — and that the institutions that built the audience deserve to be there to see it.
